content: 1. If the first rapid diagnostic test (RDT 1) is reactive and the first immunoassay (IA 1) is non-reactive, or if RDT 1 is non-reactive and IA 1 is reactive, further testing should be conducted using a second RDT (RDT 2) or a second immunoassay (IA 2) to confirm the results. 2. In cases where RDT 1 is reactive and IA 1 is also reactive, the result is considered positive, and no further testing is required. 3. If RDT 1 is non-reactive and IA 1 is also non-reactive, the result is considered negative, and no further testing is needed. 4. For verification studies, each specimen in the verification panel must be labeled with a unique identification number that does not reveal the expected result. This ensures diagnostic accuracy and prevents bias. 5. Test operators should be blinded to the expected reference results for each specimen to maintain the integrity of the testing process. 6. Aliquots of specimens should only be removed from storage when they are ready to be tested to preserve their integrity. 7. Testing should be performed strictly according to the instructions provided with the test kit, including the instructions for use (IFU), labels, and other instructional materials. 8. Test operators should represent the intended users of the test and should perform the testing without assistance. 9. If test kit controls are available, either within the kit or separately, they must be used in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. 10. Both lots of each product should be tested on the same verification panel to ensure consistency. 11. For visually read assays, such as RDTs, the intensity of the test band should be recorded on a scale to distinguish between weak and strong test lines: 0 (non-reactive), 1+ (weakly reactive), 2+ (moderately reactive), and 3+ (strongly reactive). 12. Results from visually read assays should be interpreted by a second blinded reader after the first reader has recorded their interpretation. This helps quantify variability due to faint test lines. 13. If the two readers agree on the test result, the status of the specimen is recorded as is. If they disagree, a third reader should adjudicate, and the majority result (two out of three) is taken as final. 14. If a conclusive result cannot be reached, the result should be recorded as inconclusive, and the specimen should be retested using a new test device from the same lot. 15. Inconclusive results should be included in the data analysis as misdiagnosed specimens. 16. Invalid test results for visually read assays typically occur when the control line does not appear, regardless of the test line, or when high background color obscures the result window. Other anomalies, such as streaking, non-migration of the specimen, or debris on the membrane, should also be recorded. 17. For instrument-based assays, invalid results occur when internal or external test kit controls (HIV-negative or HIV-positive) fall outside the acceptance range specified by the manufacturer. 18. The rate of invalid test results or runs should be recorded as a proportion of the total number of tests or runs performed. 19. Data analysis should include calculating the rate of common false reactivity between candidate products using HIV-negative specimens. If no combination of products avoids shared false-reactive results, the combination with the fewest shared false-reactive results should be chosen. 20. Sensitivity for each candidate product should be calculated using the results of HIV-antibody-positive specimens. 21. The results of the verification study should remain valid for 3–5 years. The verified testing algorithm must be reviewed every 3–5 years to determine if a new verification study is needed. 22. Testing algorithms must be continuously monitored for effectiveness, including any adverse events related to HIV misdiagnosis. 23. New testing algorithms should be implemented in parallel with existing algorithms for two weeks at high-throughput testing sites or four weeks at low-throughput sites. A discrepancy rate of >1% between new and existing algorithms requires investigation of the root cause. 24. After the initial familiarization period, new testing algorithms may be rolled out more widely. Data should be collected on the rate of HIV-inconclusive status and invalid test results, with an acceptable threshold of no more than 5%. 25. Any observations related to test procedures or operational characteristics that do not meet the manufacturer’s claims should be documented and reported according to WHO guidance on post-market surveillance of in vitro diagnostics. 26. The ongoing accuracy of verified HIV testing algorithms should be monitored through post-market surveillance. 27. False-negative HIV results are typically due to one product (e.g., Assay 1) failing to detect HIV, which is difficult to identify unless an individual with known HIV-positive status undergoes retesting. WHO does not recommend retesting for HIV-positive individuals, particularly those on antiretroviral therapy (ART). 28. False-positive HIV results may be due to one or more products in the testing algorithm, typically Assay 2 or Assay 3. WHO recommends retesting before initiating ART to identify individuals incorrectly diagnosed as HIV-positive. 29. Complaints related to the products themselves should be reported to the assay manufacturer and the national regulatory authority as part of post-market surveillance.
